newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Petronas to set up university.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Petronas to set up university.

text.p: Malaysia's state-run oil company, Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas), received approval from the Education Ministry on Friday to set up the country's third corporate-owned university.
The Petronas Technology University will be run by a wholly owned subsidiary of Petronas.
Telekom Malaysia Bhd and privatised power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd set up universities after the government amended the Education Act last year to allow corporations to run them.

"I believe Petronas Technology University could become a leading university in the region one day and contribute to the government's effort to make Malaysia an education centre that will attract students from ASEAN," said Education Minister Najib Tun Razak.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) groups Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Najib said the university would help to reduce the skills shortage in the oil and gas industry in Malaysia.

Quoting figures from the Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (Malaysia National University), he said the number of foreign and local graduates in these fields was 2,395 in 1993, against industry demand for 6,413.

"With the availability of more higher education opportunities in the country, the government will reduce the number of students to be sent abroad, thus limiting foreign exchange outflows as well as preventing students from being exposed to the influence of foreign culture," Najib told reporters at the event.

Some 60,000 Malaysians studied abroad in 1994 -- nearly a quarter of the total enrolled in higher education. It cost the country 2.5 billion ringgit ($1 billion), or about a quarter of Malaysia's current account deficit that year.

"In the short to medium term, we will have to continue to send students abroad, as our needs for graduates are high," Najib said. "We will have to increase the capacity of local universities, but we will have to give them time to do this."

Najib also said the current policy was to encourage students to complete their first degrees in Malaysia. In future, students would be sent to foreign universities on a more selective basis depending on their academic performance.
Petronas President Hassan Marican, who received the letter of approval from Najib, said he expected the intake of students to be 1,000 a year by 2000.

In May, the government's Economic Planning Unit said it planned to triple its enrolment of students in science and technology courses over the next five years to meet the demands of a more sophisticated economy.
EPU officials said the enrolment into these courses would increase to 230,000 in 2000 from 89,219 in 1995.
